# PR: fix(op-reth cli): enable `debug_verbosity`/`debug_vmodule` by gating log reload on the debug namespace

**Target:** `ethereum-optimism/optimism` — `rust/op-reth` (branch `develop`)
**Files:** `rust/op-reth/crates/cli/src/{commands/mod.rs, app.rs, lib.rs}` (+67 / −1)

## Summary

`debug_verbosity` and `debug_vmodule` (runtime log-level control, added upstream in reth [#21497](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/21497)) fail on op-reth even when the `debug` RPC namespace is enabled:

```
$ curl -s $RPC -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"debug_verbosity","params":[3]}'
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"error":{"code":-32603,"message":"Log filter reload not available"}}
$ curl -s $RPC -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"debug_vmodule","params":[""]}'
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"error":{"code":-32603,"message":"Log filter reload not available"}}
```

geth returns `result: null` for the same calls. Note the code is `-32603` (internal error), **not** `-32601` (method not found) — the methods are registered and served; only the runtime reload handle is missing.

## Root cause

The reloadable log-filter layer that backs these methods is installed only when `RethTracer` is initialized with `enable_reload = true`. The Ethereum CLI wires this to whether the `debug` namespace is served:

```rust
// crates/ethereum/cli — Cli::init_tracing
let enable_reload = self.command.debug_namespace_enabled();
self.logs.init_tracing_with_layers(layers, enable_reload)?;
```

op-reth's CLI (`crates/cli/src/app.rs`) has its own `init_tracing` that hardcodes `false`:

```rust
self.guard = Some(self.cli.logs.init_tracing_with_layers(layers, false)?);
```

So the reload handle is never installed → `reth_tracing::log_handle_available()` stays `false` → `set_log_verbosity`/`set_log_vmodule` return `Err("Log filter reload not available")` → `-32603`. This is an omission when the op-reth CLI was split from the shared init path, not an intentional disable.

## Fix

Mirror the Ethereum CLI: add `Commands::debug_namespace_enabled()` and use it in `init_tracing`.

```rust
// commands/mod.rs
pub fn debug_namespace_enabled(&self) -> bool {
    matches!(self, Self::Node(cmd) if cmd.rpc.is_namespace_enabled(RethRpcModule::Debug))
}
// app.rs
let enable_reload = self.cli.command.debug_namespace_enabled();
self.guard = Some(self.cli.logs.init_tracing_with_layers(layers, enable_reload)?);
```

No `Cargo.toml` change: `reth-rpc-server-types` (providing `RethRpcModule` / `RpcServerArgs::is_namespace_enabled`) is already a dependency of the cli crate.

## Behavior

- `debug` reachable on any transport — incl. IPC, which is on by default and `is_namespace_enabled` treats as exposing every namespace — ⇒ reloadable layer installed ⇒ `debug_verbosity(level)` / `debug_vmodule(pattern)` return `null` and take effect at runtime.
- Otherwise (e.g. `--ipcdisable` and no `debug` in http/ws api) ⇒ unchanged, layer not installed.

## Test

Added `debug_namespace_gates_log_reload` unit test (cli crate): `debug` in `--http.api`, in `--ws.api`, absent + `--ipcdisable` (off), default IPC (on), and non-node command (off).

## Downstream verification

Verified on the Mantle devnet: applying this change flips `debug_verbosity([3])` and `debug_vmodule([""])` from `-32603` to `result: null`, matching op-geth. Reference implementation / evidence: mantle-xyz/reth#94.

op-node: ignore stale sequencer action after Stop

## Problem

`Sequencer.Stop()` does not fully stop the sequencer: a sequencer-action timer that the driver armed *before* the stop can still fire once afterwards.

The driver decides whether a sequencer action is wanted in exactly one place — `planSequencerAction()` — and only at the top of each event-loop iteration (`op-node/rollup/driver/driver.go:311`). Once it arms `sequencerTimer` and parks in the `select` (`driver.go:324`), `Stop()` (running in the admin-RPC goroutine) can flip the sequencer's `nextActionOK=false`, but it cannot retract the already-armed timer or force the parked loop to re-plan. When the timer fires, the loop emits `SequencerActionEvent` (`driver.go:326`) before it loops back to re-evaluate — so a *stopped* sequencer runs `onSequencerAction()` one more time, builds a block on its cached `latestHead`, and issues a forkchoice update reasserting that head.

### Why it caused reorg flakes

In the interop reorg acceptance tests, the op-test-sequencer commits a conflicting block **through op-node itself** — `CommitBlock` is op-node's own `EngineController` method (`op-node/rollup/engine/api.go:114`), which inserts the block, sets op-node's engine unsafe head, and forkchoices the EL onto it. The commit is not a rogue external write; op-node makes the block canonical.

The breakage is internal to op-node: the `EngineController` now knows the head is the new block, but the `Sequencer` subsystem still holds its stale cached `latestHead` (updated only asynchronously via `onForkchoiceUpdate`). The stale sequencer action fires in that window and forkchoices the EL back onto the old head — silently undoing a reorg that had already been made canonical.

## Fix

Guard `onSequencerAction()` on `d.active`, mirroring the intent already documented in `Stop()` (which wipes the in-flight building state specifically so a stopped sequencer can't reorg). `Sequencer.OnEvent` and `Sequencer.Stop` both take `d.l`, so this is race-free: a stopped sequencer never processes the action, regardless of how the event was emitted.

I considered a driver-side re-check (`if _, ok := s.sequencer.NextAction(); ok { emit }`) instead. It only *narrows* the window — `Stop()` can still land between the re-check and the emit — whereas the sequencer-side guard is airtight because of the shared lock. The two are complementary; the sequencer guard is the necessary/sufficient correctness fix.

## Why this fixes two issues

Every interop reorg test does the same "stop sequencer → commit a conflicting block through op-node → assert the reorg" dance, and each has had to hand-roll a `SyncStatus().UnsafeL2` quiescence wait to paper over this race. The ones that miss a spot flake:

- **#20198 `TestReorgUnsafeHead`** — its *first* `ReorgExact` (`unsafe_head_test.go:91`) samples the EL head in the raw post-commit window, before `StartSequencer` and before the quiescence wait that only guards its *second* assertion. This is the assertion that failed in CI.
- **#20943 `TestReorgInitExecMsg`** — same pattern, no quiescence guard at all.

Fixing the shared root cause in op-node removes the need for those per-test band-aids.

## Testing

- Added `TestSequencer_NoActionAfterStop` (`op-node/rollup/sequencing/sequencer_test.go`): starts→stops the sequencer, fires a stale `SequencerActionEvent`, and asserts no build job starts and no events are emitted. Confirmed it **fails without the guard** (reaches `startBuildingBlock` → emits `BuildStartEvent`) and passes with it.
- `go test ./op-node/rollup/sequencing/ ./op-node/rollup/driver/` — green.
- `go vet ./op-node/rollup/sequencing/` — clean.

## Reviewer note

This touches core sequencing (consensus-adjacent). The production impact of the pre-fix behavior is limited and self-healing (a stopped sequencer issuing one stale block-building FCU — a wasted/never-sealed build, or a brief local reorg during failover that re-follows the network), but it directly defeats the reorg tests. Would appreciate a sanity check from the sequencing owners on the guard.

## Summary

Extract the base pool-builder configuration out of `OpNode::components` into a reusable, generic method `OpNode::standard_pool_builder<T>`, so a downstream node can reuse the exact base config and only chain its own `with_ordering` / `with_validator_wrapper` on top.

Previously the base config (tx-conditional, interop endpoints and quorum, shared interop failsafe gate) was inlined in `components()`. A downstream node (e.g. op-reth-premium) that wants a policy-typed pool had to hand-copy every base `with_` call, which risks **silently dropping one** as the base config grows — as nearly happened with `with_interop_failsafe`, where a txpool writer and payload reader on different failsafe handles would desync.

## Change

```rust
pub fn standard_pool_builder<T>(&self) -> OpPoolBuilder<T> {
    OpPoolBuilder::<T>::default()
        .with_enable_tx_conditional(self.args.enable_tx_conditional)
        .with_interop(
            self.args.interop_http.clone(),
            self.args.interop_min_responses,
            self.args.interop_safety_level,
        )
        .with_interop_failsafe(self.interop_failsafe.clone())
}
```

- `components()` now calls `.pool(self.standard_pool_builder())`, `T` defaulting to `OpPooledTransaction` — **behavior is unchanged**.
- Generic over the pooled-tx type `T` on purpose: a downstream node's pool builder may be `OpPoolBuilder<CustomTx, ...>`, not the default, so a non-generic helper couldn't be chained. It composes with the `with_ordering` / `with_validator_wrapper` seams added in #21531.
- The base `with_` calls now live in exactly one place; a future base `with_` flows to every consumer on the next pin bump instead of being silently missed.

- `standard_pool_builder_forwards_base_config` — sets every base field to a non-default value and asserts each is forwarded; proves the interop failsafe is a **single shared handle** by writing through the node and observing through the pool in both directions.
- `standard_pool_builder_preserves_base_config_when_chaining_seams` — asserts base config survives after chaining `with_ordering` / `with_validator_wrapper`, and that the chained ordering/validator members land.

# fix(kona,security): close three unauthenticated attack surfaces

**Type:** security fix
**Scope:** `rust/kona/`
**Base branch:** `develop`
**Head branch (in fork):** `security/kona-triple-fix-2026-07-12`
**Companion disclosure:** public 0-day gist (linked in the first comment)

## Summary

This PR closes three live, unauthenticated attack surfaces in the Rust OP Stack consensus client. Each bug is disclosed publicly in the linked gist; each is addressed here with a minimal, targeted patch plus a regression test.

| # | Class | File(s) touched | Commit |
|---|---|---|---|
| **B1** | Cross-client L2 state divergence | `crates/protocol/protocol/src/batch/bits.rs`, `crates/protocol/protocol/src/batch/errors.rs` | 3e84f427 |
| **B2** | Unbounded snappy decompression → OOM-kill | `crates/node/gossip/src/config.rs` | 837a8ccc |
| **B3** | Unauthenticated admin JSON-RPC on public bind | `crates/node/service/src/service/node.rs`, `bin/node/src/flags/rpc.rs`, `crates/node/rpc/src/admin.rs`, `crates/node/rpc/src/config.rs` | 8b1d0634 |

All three are live at `develop` HEAD `a71cadff` (2026-07-11 17:45 UTC). Under Upgrade 18 + Karst (Sepolia 2026-06-17), `CANNON_KONA` is the respected fault-proof program by default on every OP Stack chain, so B1's cross-client divergence in Kona-in-Cannon can decide dispute games. B2 and B3 compound the impact by knocking challengers offline and injecting divergent unsafe heads during the dispute window.

## B1 — reject truncated span-batch bitlist (commit 3e84f427)

`SpanBatchBits::decode` silently zero-padded truncated input. Op-node's parallel `decodeSpanBatchBits` uses `io.ReadFull` and returns `io.ErrUnexpectedEOF` for the same input, so Kona and op-node diverge on the same L1 calldata. For a legacy transaction with `protected_bits = [0x01]`, truncating the byte flips the EIP-155 protection flag from `true` to `false` in Kona while op-node rejects the batch entirely — different derived L2 state.

**Fix:** add `SpanBatchError::BitfieldTooShort` and return it when `b.len() < buffer_len`.

**Test:** `decode_rejects_truncated_input` covers empty input at `bit_length=1` and 1-byte input at `bit_length=16`; `decode_accepts_full_input` covers the positive case.

## B2 — bound gossipsub snappy pre-alloc by `MAX_GOSSIP_SIZE` (commit 837a8ccc)

`compute_message_id` (the gossipsub `message_id_fn`, invoked on every inbound PUBLISH before signature validation) called `snap::raw::Decoder::decompress_vec(&msg.data)` unconditionally. `decompress_vec` pre-allocates `vec![0; decompress_len(input)]` — up to `u32::MAX` (~4 GiB) — before inspecting any frame content. A 7-byte snappy frame declaring `u32::MAX` decompressed length forces the process into `handle_alloc_error` (SIGABRT) or the Linux OOM killer (SIGKILL). Amplification: **613,566,756×**. Persistent restart-loop; gossipsub mesh (`mesh_D = 8`) fans out.

**Fix:** pre-check `snap::raw::decompress_len(&msg.data) <= MAX_GOSSIP_SIZE` before calling `decompress_vec`, matching op-node's `BuildMsgIdFn` in `op-node/p2p/gossip.go`. Oversized headers take the invalid-snappy hash branch without allocating.

**Test:** `compute_message_id_rejects_snappy_bomb_without_alloc` feeds the exact 7-byte bomb payload `[0xFF, 0xFF, 0xFF, 0xFF, 0x0F, 0x00, 0x41]` and asserts that the invalid-snappy branch is taken.

**Sibling site (not touched in this PR, but flagged for follow-up):** `rust/op-alloy/crates/rpc-types-engine/src/envelope.rs::decode_v{1,2,3,4}` share the same primitive. Fix upstream in `op-alloy`.

## B3 — gate admin RPC, restrict `admin_postUnsafePayload`, default bind to `127.0.0.1` (commit 8b1d0634)

Four related sub-fixes in one commit:

1. **`crates/node/service/src/service/node.rs`** — Gate the `AdminRpc::new(...).into_rpc()` merge on `config.enable_admin()`. Previously merged unconditionally on every Kona node, while `dev_enabled()` and `ws_enabled()` on adjacent lines already had this gate.

## Suggested review order

1. `crates/protocol/protocol/src/batch/errors.rs` — one line, adds the new error variant.
2. `crates/protocol/protocol/src/batch/bits.rs` — the B1 fix + tests.

## Backport recommendation

All three fixes should be backported to any release branch that ships Kona for Upgrade-18-compliant chains, and to any downstream OP Stack Rust fork (op-reth, op-rbuilder, Base Azul, and others) that inherited the vulnerable code shapes.

## Compatibility notes

- **B1:** breaking behavior change — batches that were previously silently zero-padded will now be rejected. This aligns Kona with op-node's canonical behavior; any node currently divergent because of the leniency was already producing a wrong state.
- **B2:** no behavior change on valid gossipsub traffic; oversized-header messages now take the invalid-snappy hash branch (which was already the fallback for decompression failure).

## Summary

Adds an explicit `SKIP_SIGNER_OWNER_CHECK=true|1` override to the shared `TaskManager` signing preflight. This lets a new Safe owner presign a follow-up task before the earlier owner-addition task executes; the owner check remains enabled by default.

The bypass still rejects a zero signer or codeless target and calls `getOwners()` to validate the Safe interface. Sequential owner rotations intentionally require a newly added owner to sign a later task. For example, `056-fus-rotation-1` adds an owner that must sign `057-fus-rotation-2`, but the existing preflight reads current onchain ownership and blocks that signature until `056` executes.

perf(kona-driver): decode only the L1-info deposit when computing L2BlockInfo (recreate #21347)

<!-- ccr-slack-attribution -->
_Requested by **Adrian Sutton** · [Slack thread](https://oplabs-pbc.slack.com/archives/D0AGFDD2MEE/p1783986050103609)_

This recreates #21347 (by @karlb), rebased cleanly onto the latest `develop`. The original commits are preserved with their authorship.

### Rebase note

The original PR's 5th commit, `perf(kona-sp1-client-utils): compute L2BlockInfo without decoding all txs` (`346122d`), was **dropped** as obsolete. It ported the optimization into the SP1 range program's *own copy* of the driver advance loop in `rust/kona/sp1/crates/client/src/client.rs`. Since #21347 was opened, `develop` deleted that duplicate loop: the SP1 client was refactored to a `WitnessExecutor` that calls the shared `kona_driver::Driver` (`advance_to_target_with_metrics` in `witness/executor.rs`). The SP1 client therefore now inherits the optimization transitively from the `kona-driver` changes in this PR, and there is no longer a `client.rs` to patch (it was a modify/delete conflict against a deleted file). The remaining 5 commits applied cleanly.

## Description

After executing a payload, `Driver::advance_to_target` RLP-decodes **every transaction in every derived block** — bytes the executor has already decoded and validated once — solely so `L2BlockInfo::from_block_and_genesis` can read `transactions[0]`. Inside the FPVM those cycles are real cost. It also rebuilds an `OpBlock` whose header is then re-hashed via `hash_slow()`, even though the driver already holds the sealed header from the execution outcome.

The first transaction of every non-genesis L2 block is the L1-info deposit, which is protocol-shared across OP Stack chains — the same function already hardcodes the `0x7E` type byte in the Holocene deposit-only retry path. So decode just that one transaction:

1. **`feat(kona-protocol)`**: add `L2BlockInfo::from_header_and_first_tx(&Sealed<Header>, Option<&Bytes>, &ChainGenesis)`, mirroring `from_block_and_genesis` for callers that hold a sealed header and raw EIP-2718 transaction bytes rather than a decoded block:
   - The block hash is taken from the seal instead of recomputed; the caller must guarantee the seal is the header's true hash (debug-asserted).
   - The first transaction is classified by its type byte *before* decoding, so chains with extended (non-OP-decodable) transaction envelopes get a descriptive `FirstTxNonDeposit` error rather than an RLP failure; only a potential deposit or legacy transaction is actually decoded, strictly (`decode_2718_exact`, trailing bytes rejected).
   - At the genesis block the first transaction is not inspected at all, matching `from_block_and_genesis`.
   - Both constructors share a private `from_block_info_and_first_tx` core, so they cannot drift apart.
2. **`perf(kona-driver)`**: replace the `OpBlock` assembly in `advance_to_target` with the new constructor, fed by `attributes.transactions.first()`. The O(n) decode, the `BlockBody` construction, and the redundant keccak all go away. The seal contract the driver now relies on is documented on `Executor::execute_payload`; the trait is otherwise untouched.
3. **`chore(kona-driver)!`**: remove the now-unconstructable `DriverError::Rlp` variant and the `alloy-rlp` dependency. Breaking for code matching exhaustively on `DriverError`.

A side effect worth noting: chains with extended transaction envelopes (e.g. Celo's CIP-64) can use `kona_driver::Driver` unmodified, since the driver no longer decodes the full transaction list as `OpTxEnvelope`.

## Tests

- New unit tests for `from_header_and_first_tx`: equivalence with `from_block_and_genesis` on the same block; genesis handling (hash match/mismatch, first transaction ignored at the genesis block); error paths (missing first tx, empty bytes, non-deposit type byte, valid legacy tx rejected as non-deposit, garbage RLP list/string prefixes, malformed deposit payload, trailing bytes after a valid deposit).
- Original PR reported `cargo nextest run --all-features` green for `kona-protocol` and `kona-driver` (225 passed) and clean clippy + nightly fmt.

op-deployer: estimate broadcast gas against the target chain (Glamsterdam/EIP-8037)

> **Stacked on #21727** (`joshklop/op-geth-bal`). Review/merge that first; this PR's base is that branch, not `develop`.

## Problem

Deploying the OP Stack with op-deployer onto a **post-Glamsterdam L1** fails: any transaction that deploys contract code loops on

```
failed to call: contract creation code storage out of gas
```

and the deploy never completes. Reproduced cleanly with a fresh deployer running `bootstrap superchain` against a `glamsterdam-devnet-6` L1 (post-Amsterdam): it lands one tx, then wedges.

## Root cause

op-deployer sizes each broadcast transaction's gas limit from the gas used by its **in-process script simulator**, which is pinned to a **Cancun-era** gas schedule (`op-chain-ops/script/script.go`: `CancunTime=0`, `PragueTime=nil`, no Osaka/Amsterdam) and therefore charges the legacy **200 gas/byte** code-deposit cost.

Glamsterdam's **[EIP-8037 (State Creation Gas Cost Increase)](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-8037)** raises the code-deposit cost to **`CPSB = 1530` gas/byte (~7.65×)**. So the simulated `GasUsed` for anything that stores contract code is ~8× too low. `padGasLimit`'s 1.2× pad can't bridge that; because the gas limit is explicitly set, `txmgr` validates it with `eth_call` (`estimateOrValidateCandidateTxGas`), which reverts, and the send retries forever.

Measured on the devnet L1 (`eth_estimateGas`, marginal): **~1542 gas/byte** post-Amsterdam vs 200 legacy; a 24 KB contract went from ~4.9M to **~36.9M gas** to deploy.

## Scope — every deploy flow, not just bootstrap

This bites any flow that stores contract code, whether **directly** or **indirectly**:

| Flow | How it deploys | Broadcast type |
|---|---|---|
| `bootstrap superchain` / `bootstrap implementations` | `new X()` / CREATE2 | `Create` / `Create2` |
| `apply` (deploy an L2 chain) | `opcm.deploy(config)` — a CALL to OPCM that CREATEs the chain's contracts internally (`DeployOPChain.s.sol`) | `Call` |
| `manage migrate` | CALL into OPCM | `Call` |

So the fix must cover **calls** as well as creations — an earlier creation-only version would have missed `apply`.

## Fix

Size each broadcast's gas limit as **`max(live eth_estimateGas, simulated)`**, clamped to the block gas limit, **for all broadcast types**, falling back to the simulated estimate on estimation error.

- The live estimate reflects the chain's actual gas rules (EIP-8037 included).
- Keeping the simulated value as a floor / fallback means a broadcast that depends on an earlier, not-yet-mined transaction in the same bundle (whose live estimate may revert or read low) is **never worse than the previous behaviour**.
- The estimation `CallMsg` leaves `Gas` unset so the node bounds its search by the **block gas limit** rather than the `2^24` per-tx cap (`params.MaxTxGas`), which large post-Amsterdam deploys exceed.

## Verification

- New unit test `TestEstimatedGasLimit` (stubbed estimator): live estimate wins for creations and calls; clamps to the block gas limit; never drops below simulated; falls back on error; CREATE2 targets the deterministic deployer with salt-prefixed data; calls estimate against the call target.
- Live evidence on a `glamsterdam-devnet-6` L1: reproduced the failure with the released op-deployer; `eth_estimateGas` returns the correct ~37M for a 24 KB creation and a raw deploy at that limit succeeds (chain accepts it; live-estimate path is sound).
- ⚠️ Full end-to-end `bootstrap` + `apply` on a post-Amsterdam L1 with a locally-built binary is **not yet run here** (needs the contracts-artifacts build); recommend confirming in CI / a devnet run before un-drafting.

## Follow-up (not in this PR)

The deeper fix is to make op-deployer's script simulator use the **target chain's** fork schedule (incl. EIP-8037) so simulated gas matches on-chain gas, removing the need to re-estimate live. That's blocked on go-ethereum implementing the EIP-8037 gas rules and should be coordinated with the op-geth work in #21727.

## Summary

Bumps the `github.com/ethereum/go-ethereum` → `op-geth` `replace` to the head of ethereum-optimism/op-geth#804, which adds the EIP-7928 `BlockAccessListHash` field to the block header and its RLP/hash calculation.

## Why

The pinned op-geth (`v1.101702.3-rc.4`) predates EIP-7928, so its `types.Header` has no `BlockAccessListHash` field. On a post-Amsterdam (Glamsterdam) L1, `Header.Hash()` therefore RLP-hashes an incomplete header and produces a block hash that never existed on chain. op-node identifies L1 blocks by `Header.Hash()`, so every post-fork L1 block becomes unfetchable (`querying block: not found`) and op-node wedges at the fork boundary — both the sequencer and derivation stall. (It also surfaces as a spurious `possible L1 re-org` every slot, because op-node's linear-extension check compares a correctly-read parent hash against its own incorrectly-computed head hash.)

With op-geth#804, `Header.Hash()` matches the chain again and op-node follows L1 cleanly across the Glamsterdam boundary.

## Testing

- op-node builds against the bumped op-geth.
- Verified end-to-end on an ethpandaops `glamsterdam-devnet-6` devnet: with this op-geth, op-node crosses the L1 Glamsterdam (Amsterdam/Gloas) fork boundary — the unsafe head keeps advancing and derivation continues (blob DA served by a Gloas-capable CL). Without it, op-node wedges at the first post-Amsterdam block.

## Note

Points at a pseudo-version of the op-geth#804 head commit. **Blocked on op-geth#804** — re-pin to a release tag before merge.

fix(op-revm): discard journal after non-deposit tx errors (SDM warm-set leak)

## Summary

`OpHandler::catch_error` reset the EVM journal only on the **deposit** error path. For a **non-deposit** transaction that fails validation (e.g. `NonceTooLow`, or EIP-3607 contract-sender), it returned without calling `journal.discard_tx()`, so the failed tx's partial state — including its **EIP-2929 warm/cold access stamps** — persisted in the shared journal and leaked into the next transaction executed on the same EVM.

On the **SDM `Produce`** execution path (which routes through `inspect_tx`, skipping `finalize()` on error), this means a builder can bill a later included tx a **warm** account access for a tx that never entered the block. A validator re-executing the canonical block (commit-only, `Verify` mode) never ran the skipped tx, recomputes the access as **cold**, and gets a different gas result → **builder-vs-validator divergence → block rejection**.

## Fix

Add the missing `else` branch in `OpHandler::catch_error` calling `journal.discard_tx()` on non-deposit errors, matching upstream revm's `EthHandler::catch_error`. One line of behavior; `rust/op-revm/src/handler.rs`.

This mirrors the same fix independently made upstream in [bluealloy/revm#3780](https://github.com/bluealloy/revm/pull/3780) and in Base's EVM fork ([base/base#3806](https://github.com/base/base/pull/3806)). Note that pulling in revm #3780 alone does **not** fix this on the OP path, because `op-revm` overrides `catch_error`.

## Exposure

Not exploitable on chains running today: with SDM disabled (the current production config) execution uses the `transact` path, whose `finalize()` runs even on error and wipes the failed tx's journal. The leak surfaces only once SDM (`Produce` mode) is active.

## Regression coverage

Two layers, both trigger variants (`NonceTooLow` and EIP-3607), each verified **red without the fix** (2500-gas divergence) and **green with it**:

- **`rust/alloy-op-evm/src/block/tests.rs`** — builder(`Produce`)-vs-validator(`Verify`) block-executor divergence, plus an SDM-disabled safety guard.
- **`rust/op-rbuilder/.../builders/context.rs`** — the sequencer builder's `execute_best_transactions` selection loop: a skipped failed candidate must not warm a later included tx.

## Test plan

- [x] `cargo test -p alloy-op-evm --lib block::tests::sdm::warmleak`
- [x] `cargo test -p op-rbuilder --lib builders::context::tests::skipped`
- [x] Each new test confirmed red against the unfixed handler, green against the fix.

fix(op-reth): reserve Isthmus operator fee in tx-pool balance check

## Description

Fixes #21608.

`OpTransactionValidator::apply_op_checks` reserved only the **L1 data fee** on top of the intrinsic tx cost when checking sender balance at pool admission. Post-Isthmus, execution additionally charges the **operator fee** up front from the sender's balance, sized by the tx gas limit (`L1BlockInfo::tx_cost` → `operator_fee_charge`, gated on `spec.is_enabled_in(ISTHMUS)`). A sender funded for `gas × maxFee + value + L1 data fee` but not the operator fee was therefore admitted to the pool and propagated, but the tx could never execute — wasted pool space and propagation bandwidth, and an admission-parity gap vs op-geth, whose pool does charge it (`NewOperatorCostFunc` / `TotalTxCost` in `core/txpool/validation.go`).

## Changes

- `apply_op_checks`: when Isthmus is active at the tracked block timestamp **and** both operator fee params are present, add `operator_fee_charge(&encoded, U256::from(gas_limit), spec)` to the reserved cost. The spec is derived per-timestamp via `revm_spec_by_timestamp_after_bedrock`, so the Jovian formula change is handled automatically.
- The params-present guard is load-bearing: `operator_fee_charge` panics (`.expect()`) on unset params, which is the validator's state before the first post-Isthmus L1-info block is tracked (e.g. boot at genesis). In that window no fee is reserved, matching current behavior until the first block updates the tracked info.
- Gas limit is the worst-case charge, matching op-geth's `tx.Gas()` and execution's upfront deduction exactly.

Scope: pool admission only — no block-validation, execution, or state-root change. The sibling admission gap (#21546, missing `EffectiveGasLimit` / `l1InfoGasOverhead` reservation) is intentionally not bundled.

## Tests

Three new unit tests in `validator.rs` (in-module, to seed the tracked `L1BlockInfo` operator fee params):

- `operator_fee_short_balance_is_rejected` — balance one wei short of `cost + operator_fee` → rejected with insufficient funds. Fails without the fix (tx is admitted), passes with it.
- `operator_fee_covered_balance_is_accepted` — exact balance → valid.
- `missing_operator_fee_params_do_not_panic_or_reserve` — post-Isthmus timestamp with untracked params → no panic, tx accepted.

Verified locally: `cargo test -p reth-optimism-txpool -p reth-optimism-primitives --all-features` (59 + 27 passed), rustfmt (pinned nightly) clean, `cargo clippy --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings` clean on both crates.

op-node: move follow-source requests off the driver loop

## Summary

Two commits, structured so the regression is directly demonstrable:

1. **`op-acceptance-tests`: regression test (fails at that commit).** A stallable reverse proxy is interposed in front of a light CL sequencer's follow-source endpoint and switched to hold all requests without responding. The test requires unsafe block production to continue with no gap over 8s during a 30s observation window — strictly below the follow-source client's 10s call timeout (the guaranteed production dead window when follow requests block the driver loop), well above the healthy 2s cadence.
2. **`op-node`: the fix (makes the test pass).** Run the follow-source status + L1 request sequence in a background goroutine, keep at most one fetch in flight (ticks during a fetch are coalesced), and deliver validated status snapshots back to the driver loop, which applies all side effects (L1 status event, success metric, engine `FollowSource`) in the original order.

To see the regression: check out the first commit and run the test — block production freezes the moment the follow tick fires.

## Why

`followUpstream` performs its upstream status request and up to four sequential L1 lookups directly in the driver's main `select` loop. Slow or unresponsive RPCs prevent the loop from servicing sequencer actions and block production. Request order, validation checks, failure metrics, and RPC client timeouts are unchanged; no caching or request deduplication is introduced. Engine reconciliation intentionally stays on the driver loop.

## Verification

Both runs on this machine (macOS, sysgo devstack, op-reth ELs):

- **Without fix** (first commit): `FAIL` in 42s — `chain 901 latest head stalled at block 17: no new block for 8.006s (max allowed 8s)`. The proxy held the follow request, the RPC client timed out at exactly +10s, and production froze for the full window.
- **With fix** (second commit): `PASS` — 15 blocks in the 30s window (perfect 2s cadence) while 3 follow-source requests were held by the stalled proxy (each timing out client-side at 10s, single-flight coalescing the ticks in between).
- `go test -race ./op-node/rollup/driver ./op-node/node` — unit tests pin the async delivery, the L1 request order, and the exactly-one-result-per-fetch liveness contract the single-flight flag depends on.

## Test infra added (first commit)

- `sysgo.StallableProxy` / `StallableFollowSourceProxies`: reverse proxy that can hold requests open on demand, wired via an `L2CLOption` that wraps any CL's follow-source URL; counts held requests so the test cannot pass vacuously
- the light-sequencer preset accepts `GlobalL2CLOptions` (its runtime already plumbed them; only the option-validation mask blocked them)
- `dsl.L2ELNode.KeptAdvancing`: requires a head to advance continuously — unlike `Advanced`, a stall followed by a catch-up burst is a failure

Supersedes #21757 (same op-node change, previously on a fork) with review fixups folded in: removed the now write-only `Driver.syncConfig` field, documented the fetch/apply split contract, added unit tests for the nil-on-failure delivery.

[codex] move follow-source requests off driver loop

## Summary

- run the existing follow-source status and L1 request sequence in a background operation
- allow at most one follow-source request sequence to be in flight
- return successful status snapshots to the driver loop for event emission, metrics, and engine reconciliation

## Why

`followUpstream` currently performs its upstream status request and up to four sequential L1 lookups directly in the driver's main `select` loop. Slow RPCs therefore prevent the loop from servicing sequencer actions and can delay block production.

This change removes those external requests from the driver hot path while retaining the existing request order, validation checks, failure metrics, and RPC client timeouts.

## Impact

The driver loop remains responsive to sequencer timers while follow-source inputs are being fetched. Ticks that occur while a fetch is active are coalesced by the single-flight guard.

Engine reconciliation intentionally remains on the driver loop. This PR does not add caching, deduplicate or parallelize L1 requests, or change timeout behavior.

## Tests

- `go test ./op-node/rollup/driver ./op-node/node`
- `go test ./op-node/...`
- `go test -race ./op-node/rollup/driver`
- `just --unstable lint-go`

## Summary

- deduplicate follow-source L1 origin lookups by block number
- resolve unique origins concurrently against the configured L1 RPC
- fetch upstream status and L1 origins in a single-flight background worker
- cap the complete network-fetch round at two seconds
- apply validated labels and mutate engine state only on the driver event loop

## Why

`followUpstream` previously fetched upstream status and validated local-safe, safe, finalized, and current L1 origins with synchronous calls in the driver's main select loop. Duplicate or slow requests could therefore delay sequencer actions.

The updated path preserves fresh, independent canonical-L1 validation while issuing at most one lookup per unique block number and bounding aggregate lookup latency instead of accumulating the timeout of each call. A single background fetch may be active at a time; completed immutable results return to the driver loop for validation metrics, event emission, and engine reconciliation.

## Impact

Follow-mode sequencers issue fewer L1 network requests when labels share an origin. Upstream and L1 network latency no longer blocks the sequencer timer. A slow fetch round fails after two seconds and retries on a later poll without accepting unverified upstream labels.

- `go test ./op-node/rollup/driver ./op-node/node`
- `go test ./op-node/...`
- `just --unstable lint-go`

## Summary

- preserve physical EIP-2718 prefix presence in Kona span-batch transaction-data parsing
- keep a leading `0x00` so the downstream typed decoder rejects it instead of reinterpreting the payload as a prefixless legacy transaction

## Root cause

Kona inferred prefix presence from the logical `OpTxType`. Because legacy is represented as `0`, a physically present `0x00` was consumed and then dropped. That allowed the following valid legacy payload to be accepted as a prefixless legacy transaction.

Update Alloy's `TransactionEnvelope` derive macro to model legacy explicitly (for example, `#[envelope(legacy)]`). This can preserve `Legacy = 0` for metadata and RPC while making `typed_decode(0, ...)` reject the reserved EIP-2718 value.

test(op-acceptance): settle light-seq cross-safe before EL safe assert

## Summary

De-flakes `TestSupernodeLightSequencerInteropInvalidMessageReplacement` (job `memory-all-opn-op-reth`, ~2.4% fail rate — 2/82 job runs over 200 `develop` pipelines; most recent failure was pipeline 129922).

## Root cause

The light op-node is both a **sequencer** and a **follow-source follower**. After the invalid-message reorg, the fresh transfer sent by `ResendUntilSafe` re-diverges the light sequencer's unsafe head from the supernode's upstream safe chain. `EngineController.FollowSource` reorgs onto the upstream via `forceReset` (the #21119 / #21155 fix), but the sequencer rebuilds a block on its own fork before the next ~2s upstream poll lands the FCU — so recovery becomes a **ratcheting oscillation**: every other poll cycle adopts the upstream safe head, the alternate cycle resets `local-safe` back to genesis before re-adopting. Net advance is ~1 block per two cycles (~4s/block).

The final assertion `sys.L2ELB.Reached(eth.Safe, settledBlock, 30)` gives the light EL's `safe` forkchoice pointer 60s (30 × 2s) to reach the target. On a shard that loses the race, that budget can expire with the EL's safe still short of `settledBlock`, even though the supernode's own L1-derived safe head is well ahead. In pipeline 129922 the light EL safe was pinned at 26 (target 30) while the supernode's derived safe reached 61.

Convergence is **bounded, not stalled** — the sibling chain converged in the same run — so this is a race to be settled, not a liveness bug to work around.

## Fix

Gate on the light CL's cross-safe reaching `settledBlock` before polling the EL:

```go
sys.L2BCL.Reached(safety.CrossSafe, settledBlock, 45)
```

The EL's `safe` forkchoice pointer only advances once the CL emits the FCU for that cross-safe head, so waiting for the CL to converge first removes the race. The 45-attempt (90s) budget is sized to the measured ~4s/block oscillation rate. This mirrors the existing cross-safe settle gate earlier in the scenario.

## Follow-up (not in this PR)

This is a test-side fix. The underlying follow-source ↔ sequencer oscillation still costs real light-sequencer followers a wasted reset on every other poll cycle during divergence recovery; making `FollowSource`'s `forceReset` resist being clobbered by the next sequencer build would roughly halve convergence time. Worth a separate op-node issue.

## Testing

- `go vet` and `gofmt` clean.
- **Not run locally**: this test requires a built `op-reth` binary; runtime validation is via CI. Given the ~2.4% base rate, CI green across re-runs is the meaningful signal.

Follow-up to #21753 (merged). Two counters:
- **`kona_node_gossip_invalid_message{reason}`** — block-handler rejections before validation: `oversized_snappy`, `decode_error`, `unknown_topic` (mutually exclusive per message).

Its own counter, not a shared `reason`, because it overlaps the handler reasons for the same message and counts on a larger denominator.

Messages that decode but fail block validation stay metered by the existing `BLOCK_VALIDATION_FAILED`. Every invalidation path now records a metric and a `debug!`; the invalid-block `warn!` is downgraded to `debug!` too.

## Summary

Bumps `github.com/andybalholm/brotli` v1.1.0 → v1.2.2 (the brotli decoder op-node derivation uses in `BatchReader`, `rollup/derive/channel.go:203`).

andybalholm **v1.2.0** fixed its handling of truncated streams: `Reader.Read` now returns `io.ErrUnexpectedEOF` instead of a clean `io.EOF` when the input ends before the last meta-block completes — matching the C reference (`libbrotlidec`) and **RFC 7932 §9.3** ("if the stream ends before the completion of the last meta-block, then the stream should be rejected as invalid"). v1.1.0 silently treated such truncations as a clean decode.

## This bump is behaviorally inert for derivation

It does **not** change consensus behavior on its own:

- `ChannelInReader.NextBatch` (`channel_in_reader.go:92-100`) collapses both `io.EOF` and `io.ErrUnexpectedEOF` from the batch closure into the same `NextChannel()` + `NotEnoughData`.
- `rlp.Stream` already surfaces `ErrUnexpectedEOF` for a mid-item EOF, regardless of the underlying reader's terminal error.

**Verified empirically:** a fixed brotli channel decoded through the real `BatchReader` at v1.1.0 vs v1.2.2 — full stream + all 10,366 truncation offsets + a sampled corruption sweep — produces **byte-identical batch output** (same SHA-256).

## Why bump it then

It's a safe dependency update, and it's the **enabler** for strict channel decompression ([protocol-team#84](https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/protocol-team/issues/84)): it gives op-node the `ErrUnexpectedEOF` signal needed to *distinguish* a truncated channel, which the strict-decompression rule can then act on. That consensus-affecting rule change lives in the #84 work, not here.

## Notes

- go.sum gains `github.com/xyproto/randomstring v1.0.5` — a **test-only** transitive dep of andybalholm (import path is via `andybalholm/brotli.test`), not compiled into any op-node binary.
- Context and the broader Go↔Rust brotli decoder-conformance effort: #21793.

kona: reject leading 0x00 span-batch tx-type byte

Aligns kona's span-batch `read_tx_data` with op-node on a leading `0x00` tx-type byte.

`read_tx_data` consumed a leading `0x00` as an EIP-2718 type prefix and, because `OpTxType::try_from(0x00) = Legacy`, decoded the *following* bytes as a legacy transaction. op-node instead keeps the `0x00` and rejects it as an unsupported typed-tx envelope (`decodeTyped` has no `0x00` case), so the two derivation implementations disagreed on identical span-batch bytes.

The fix rejects a *consumed* type prefix that resolves to `Legacy`: a legacy tx has no prefix, so its first byte is an RLP list header (`0xc0..`), never a type identifier. Prefixless legacy txs are unchanged. After this, kona's accepted tx-type set (`legacy`, `0x01`, `0x02`, `0x04`, `0x7D`) matches op-node's `decodeTyped` exactly.

Consensus-affecting (derivation): deploying to a live chain requires a new kona-client release + prestate.

Adds `[00 c3 80 80 80]` as a shared conformance vector on both the kona and op-node decoders — a valid legacy tx (three empty fields) that both clients reject once a `0x00` type byte is prepended.

test(op-devstack): funder waits for balance >= target, not exact

## Problem

`TestPreNoInbox` (job `memory-all-opn-op-reth`) failed with:

```
op-acceptance-tests/tests/interop/upgrade/pre_test.go:88
  → op-devstack/dsl/funder.go (FundAtLeast → WaitForBalance)
  → op-devstack/dsl/eoa.go
Error: Condition never satisfied
Messages: awaiting balance to be updated
```

Line 88 funds a fresh EOA (`bob`) with 0.01 ETH on chain B. The wait for its balance never completed and the test timed out.

## Root cause: faucet retry funds the account twice

`dsl.Faucet.Fund` retries `RequestETH` up to 3×. `Funder.Fund` / `FundAtLeast` then wait for the EOA balance to become **exactly** the expected post-funding value (`WaitForBalance`, `==`).

In the failing run:

1. The op-reth sequencer for chain 902 stalled ~22s (`Cannot seal block, payload ID is unknown` / `Sequencer temporarily could not seal block`), producing no blocks.
2. The faucet published its funding tx at **nonce 0** (`03f306…`). The stall made the client-side `RequestETH` exceed its deadline (`context deadline exceeded`), but that nonce-0 tx stayed in the mempool.
3. The retry issued a **new** faucet tx at **nonce 1** (`e915bb…`).
4. When the sequencer recovered, **block 81 sealed with `txs=2`** — both the nonce-0 and nonce-1 transfers landed. (A nonce-1 tx cannot be included unless nonce 0 is too.)
5. `bob` therefore received the funding amount **twice → 0.02 ETH**, while `WaitForBalance` waited for exactly 0.01 ETH. The exact-match condition can never be satisfied, so it blocked until `TransactionTimeout` and failed.

`alice` on chain 901, which hit no stall, funded with a single nonce-0 tx and passed — confirming the double-submit only occurs when the sequencer stalls long enough to trip the faucet retry.

Tracked in #17298 (this is a distinct cause from the activation-boundary flake that issue's existing mitigation addressed).

## Fix

- Add `EOA.WaitForBalanceAtLeast` — waits for `balance >= v`.
- `Fund` / `FundAtLeast` use it: a funder only cares that the wallet has *enough*, so over-funding (from a retry) is harmless rather than a permanent hang.
- Remove redundant exact `WaitForBalance` calls that immediately followed `NewFundedEOA` and re-introduced the same hang one line later, in `RunOperatorFeeTest` (`operator_fee.go`) and `TestL1ToL2Deposit` (`deposit_test.go`). `NewFundedEOA` already waits for the balance, so these were dead weight; the deposit test derives its balance math from `GetBalance()`, which stays correct even when over-funded.
- `TestFaucetFund` (`faucet_test.go`) funds via `FundNoWait` (the raw `Faucet.Fund` retry path) and then waits on recipient (increasing) balances, so it is vulnerable to the same double-fund hang. Switch both waits to `WaitForBalanceAtLeast`; `>=` is safe because the balance starts below the target, and the test only needs to assert the funds arrived.
- Keep exact-match `WaitForBalance` where it is a meaningful assertion and `>=` would be wrong: **sender-side** waits whose expected balance is *below* the starting balance (e.g. `deposit_test.go`'s post-deposit L1 balance, `transfer_test.go`) — a `>=` wait would return immediately and defeat the check — and the deposit's exact L2 credit.

### Note on testing

I did not add a reproducing test: the trigger is a nondeterministic op-reth sequencer stall + faucet client-timeout race, and `WaitForBalance` needs a live EL, so there's no unit-level seam to force the double-fund deterministically. The fix is grounded in the CI-log evidence above (block 81 `txs=2`; faucet nonce 0 + nonce 1 both to the EOA) and the plain logic that an exact `==` wait cannot be satisfied under over-funding while `>=` can.

A deeper follow-up (out of scope here) is making the faucet retry idempotent so it doesn't submit a second funded tx at a new nonce.

## Before / After

**Before:** a reader following an old docs.optimism.io link — from a search result, a blog post, a forum answer, or a bookmark — had a good chance of hitting a dead end. 79 of the 454 legacy-URL redirects in `docs.json` pointed at pages that no longer exist, so the reader got a 404; another 83 bounced through two or three redirect hops before landing; and six entries were malformed (missing a leading `/`), so they either never fired or 404'd. The bad entries are concentrated in the old `/builders/**`, `/stack/**`, `/operators/**`, `/concepts/**`, and `/connect/**` URL trees — the canonical URL schemes for years, still widely linked from outside. **After:** every legacy URL lands on a real, current page (or the right external page) in a single hop. A reader following `/builders/dapp-developers/contracts/compatibility` now lands on [Differences from Ethereum](https://docs.optimism.io/op-stack/protocol/differences); `/stack/fault-proofs` lands on the [fault proofs explainer](https://docs.optimism.io/op-stack/fault-proofs/explainer); the old relay-messages tutorials land on [Relay transactions manually](https://docs.optimism.io/app-developers/tutorials/interoperability/manual-relay); and so on across all 161 fixed entries.

## How

One file changed: `docs/public-docs/docs.json`, `redirects` array only (166 lines, all `source`/`destination` values — entry count unchanged at 454). Every redirect was resolved transitively against the current page tree with a validation script, then fixed in three ways: **retargets (79)** — dead-end destinations repointed at the page that serves the same reader need today, verified to exist (where a page was genuinely retired with no successor, the nearest section landing page); **flattens (82)** — chained destinations replaced with their final resolved target so every redirect is a single hop; **malformed-entry fixes (6)** — missing leading slashes added on sources/destinations (an unslashed source never matches a URL, so those redirects were inert). After the change the script reports 453/454 entries resolving to an existing page or external URL in one hop, zero 404s, zero duplicate sources.

Deliberately left alone: `/builders/node-operators/overview` → `/operators/node-operators/rollup-node` (its fix is already in flight on ethereum-optimism/optimism#21777, which retargets both entries to `/node-operators/overview` — skipping it here avoids a conflict; once that PR lands, all 454 entries are single-hop).

**Before:** The style guide lives only at `docs/public-docs/STYLE_GUIDE.md` on GitHub. Site visitors browsing the Contribute group can't find it, `llms.txt` consumers can't discover it, and two docs.json redirects (`/connect/contribute/style-guide`, `/reference/contribute/style-guide`) bounce readers out of the site to GitHub.

## Single source of truth: move, not mirror

Per the render-vs-move decision required by the tracking issue, this is a **move**: `op-stack/contribute/style-guide.mdx` is now the canonical home, and `STYLE_GUIDE.md` is reduced to a pointer stub naming the `.mdx` source. Rationale:

- Mirroring would dual-source ~450 lines of prose — exactly what the [content guide's dual-sourcing ban](https://docs.optimism.io/op-stack/contribute/content-guide#link-dont-restate-the-dual-sourcing-ban) forbids ("requires double the effort to maintain and grows stale more quickly").
- Mintlify can't serve `STYLE_GUIDE.md` from the docs root — pages must live in the nav tree — so the `.md` file could never be the rendered source; the `.mdx` page has to exist either way, leaving "stub out the original" as the only zero-drift option.
- Precedent: the content guide (#21841) was born as an `.mdx` page under `op-stack/contribute/`; the style guide now sits beside it with the same `diataxis: reference` frontmatter.

The page content is a re-render of `STYLE_GUIDE.md`, not a rewrite: frontmatter added, the repo-file H1 dropped (Mintlify renders the frontmatter title), and repo-relative links adapted to site paths. Prose is otherwise unchanged.

contributing,ci: mandate scoped commits and enforce via CI

## Description

Replaces the [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/en/v1.0.0/) recommendation with a **mandate for the [Scoped Commits](https://scopedcommits.com) format** (`<scope>: <description>`), and enforces it through CI.

Rationale: the scope — what part of the codebase changed — is what log readers (contributors, debuggers, incident responders) actually scan for, while the type prefix is redundant with a well-written description. See [Stop Using Conventional Commits](https://sumnerevans.com/posts/software-engineering/stop-using-conventional-commits/). ~110 of the last 1000 commits on `develop` already use scope-first subjects.

### Changes

- **CONTRIBUTING.md**: new `### Commit messages` section mandating the format, with scope guidance (comma-separated multi-scopes, `all` for tree-wide) and links to the rationale.
- **rust/op-alloy/CONTRIBUTING.md**: same convention, replacing its Conventional Commits guidance.
- **`.github/workflows/pr-title.yml`** (new): validates the PR title on `opened/edited/reopened/synchronize`. For single-commit PRs it also validates the commit subject, since `squash_merge_commit_title: COMMIT_OR_PR_TITLE` uses that as the squash title. SHA-pinned actions, `contents: read`, title passed via `env`, no path filter so the check reports on every PR.
- **`.github/scripts/check-pr-title.sh`** (new): the validator. Accepts lowercase `[a-z0-9._/-]` scopes (comma-separated, no spaces) and GitHub's auto-generated `Revert "..."` titles; rejects `type(scope):` shapes and Conventional Commits types used as scopes (`feat`, `fix`, `chore`, ...). `docs` and `ci` remain valid since they are genuine areas of this repo.
- **`.github/scripts/check-pr-title-test.sh`** (new): 24-case self-test, run as the first workflow step.

`.github/cliff.toml` needs no change — it already has `conventional_commits = false` and builds changelogs from PR titles.

### Follow-ups requiring admin

- Add the `scoped-commits subject check` job to the `enforce-ci-checks-develop` ruleset's required checks to make it blocking.
- Consider disabling merge commits (`allow_merge_commit`), which bypass title-based enforcement.

kona: defer invalid span-batch tx types to the typed decoder

Stacks on #21808 (base = `codex/pr-21795-prefix-preservation`). Resolves the one inconsistency left in that PR: a leading `0x00` was preserved and deferred to the typed decoder, while `Deposit` (`0x7E`) and unknown type bytes were still rejected inline in `read_tx_data`.

This defers `Deposit` too. Now every *representable* type that isn't a valid span-batch envelope — `Legacy` (`0x00`) and `Deposit` — is kept and rejected in one place, `SpanBatchTransactionData::decode`/`decode_typed`, downstream in `full_txs`. That mirrors op-node's `ReadTxData` → `decodeTyped` deferral. The only remaining inline rejection is for a byte that maps to no `OpTxType` at all (`0x03`, `0x7F`, …), which can't be represented in the returned type — a type-forced boundary, not a special case.

One-line production change (drop `Ok(OpTxType::Deposit)` from the reader's reject arm). Kept the `OpTxType` return rather than switching to a raw `u8`: fully deferring unknown bytes too would have required the `u8` return + a `Vec<u8>` `tx_types` field, which added churn across `decode_tx_data`/`add_txs` for no consensus gain (unknown bytes are dropped either way).

Tests: adds a deferred-`Deposit` case and an inline-rejected unknown-byte case (`0x03`/`0x7F`), and corrects the `EIP2718_MAX_TX_TYPE` wording about which high bytes fail where (`0x80..=0xbf` at the list check; `0xff` at header decode).

Consensus-equivalence verified: for any first byte `0x00..=0xFF`, kona and op-node accept/reject the same and drop the same batches; `legacy_tx_count`/`protected_bits` sizing is unchanged (`Deposit` still isn't counted legacy). `kona-protocol` suite green; fmt + clippy clean.

- **Redirect lint** (`docs/public-docs/scripts/lint/validate-redirects.ts`): a page deleted or moved must gain a redirect in the same change (diff vs merge-base with `origin/develop`); no chained redirects; no dead redirect targets; no duplicate redirect sources (keyed on the raw source — anchor-/query-specific redirect entries are deliberate and preserved); no redirect source shadowing a live page; no internal links to non-existent paths.

Both are documented in `DOCS_CONTRIBUTING.md`.

## Enforcement: local scripts + Mintlify automation (no CI changes)

**This PR makes no `.circleci/` changes.** An earlier revision wired the lints into `ci-gate`; that wiring was removed per reviewer feedback (CI config is a shared hotspot), and enforcement moves to a [Mintlify automation](https://www.mintlify.com/docs/automations) instead:

- The scripts remain the deterministic source of truth; the automation is advisory + review-gated (it self-heals after merge — it is not a merge-blocking status check).

The 37 pre-existing violations on `develop` are grandfathered in two committed, **shrink-only** files: `scripts/lint/nav-allowlist.json` and `scripts/lint/redirect-lint-baseline.json`. The checks pass on current `develop`, fail on any new violation, and fail on stale baseline entries — so every future fix must prune its entry in the same PR and the baseline can only shrink. Fixing the existing violations (and emptying most of the baseline) is a deliberate follow-up PR under the same tracking issue, since it edits `docs.json` and is serialized behind other in-flight nav changes.

**Before:** `rust-workspace-binaries` rebuilds the full release workspace (~13.5 min) on every pipeline, gating `go-tests-short`/`go-tests-full` and the sysgo acceptance jobs — so Go-only PRs wait ~14 min for unchanged binaries, while `rust-build-op-rbuilder` skips its build in 33s via its final-binary cache.

**How:** a new reusable `rust-binary-cached-build` command in `main.yml`, wired into both `rust-workspace-binaries` invocations via `rust-build-binary`'s new `binary_cache_binaries` parameter, and into `rust-workspace-release` in rust-e2e.yml (same build parameters and consumers, so it shares the same cache key). The shell logic lives in `.circleci/scripts/rust-binary-cache.sh` with three subcommands — `compute-key` (writes the checksum inputs: sha256 of `git ls-tree -r HEAD` + the profile/features/package/binary parameters, plus the sorted binary list), `build` (hit-check, else cargo build + collect the named binaries), and `stage` (lay the binaries out for `persist_to_workspace`). Only `restore_cache`/`save_cache` remain YAML steps, as CircleCI requires. Both the hit and build paths persist exactly the named binaries at `rust/target/release/`, so downstream jobs see an identical workspace layout either way.

**Deletes the old `rust-build-vendored` job** (second commit): the job reimplemented this exact pattern inline — 134 lines, ~65 of them inline shell for the tree-hash key, hit-check, build-skip, and binary collection. `rust-build-op-rbuilder` / `rust-build-rollup-boost` now route through the same command via `rust-build-binary` (a new `extra_hash_paths` parameter covers their sibling `path`-dep closure). Net effect on this PR vs develop: **403 insertions / 178 deletions** (179 of the insertions are the script; the migration commit alone is +44/−158). Behavior deltas for the vendored builds, all intentional:

- They now restore the shared dep/toolchain caches (keyed on their own `Cargo.lock`s, which `op-rbuilder-checks`/`rollup-boost-checks` already populate), so a binary-cache miss no longer re-downloads every crate. They are restore-only (`save_cache: false`) — a single-package build must not save a partial registry under the shared key.
- Their cache key now includes the mise toolchain pins and the superchain-registry submodule pin (previously a toolchain bump did **not** invalidate the vendored binaries — a latent staleness bug), and moves from the `rust-<dir>-v9-…` namespace to `rust-workspace-bins-v1-…`, so each job rebuilds once on first run and caches thereafter.
- Binaries persist at `rust/<dir>/target/release/<bin>` — the same layout as the workspace binaries — so the `.circleci-cache/rust-binaries` special case in the sysgo consumers (`main.yml` acceptance jobs + `helpers.yml` `rust-setup-env`) is deleted too.

Job/check names are unchanged, and the workspace builds' cache key is byte-identical before and after (verified by running `compute-key` locally with the workspace parameters).

Dep-cache interplay: the command keeps the same shared dep/toolchain cache restore+save as the normal build path, so on a binary-cache miss from a rust-only change the exact-key dep cache usually hits and prepopulates the crate downloads (sccache covers recompilation, not downloads); a `Cargo.lock` change fully refreshes the dep cache per its existing no-fallback design (and also changes the binary key, landing on the build path). If the dep key was evicted while the binary key is still live, the hit path re-seeds the registry with `cargo fetch` rather than tripping #21832's empty-save guard.

feat(template): add SetFeeVaultConfig for in-place fee-vault config updates

## Summary

Adds a reusable `SetFeeVaultConfig` template that updates the on-chain config
(recipient / withdrawalNetwork / minWithdrawalAmount) of one or more L2 fee-vault
predeploys **in place**, via the vaults' own owner-gated setters
(`setRecipient` / `setWithdrawalNetwork` / `setMinWithdrawalAmount`), sent as
`OptimismPortal2.depositTransaction` from the L1 ProxyAdminOwner. No proxy upgrade,
no re-initialize. Chain-specific values come from `config.toml`.

## Why

The existing fee-vault templates change the recipient by **upgrading the impl**
(`UpdateFeeVaultRecipient` installs a new immutable impl; `FeeVaultUpgradeTemplate`
migrates to the storage design via `initialize`). Once a chain's vaults are already on the
storage design (e.g. OP Sepolia / Ink Mainnet: L1FeeVault v1.6.1, OperatorFeeVault v1.1.1),
re-running `FeeVaultUpgradeTemplate` reverts (`InvalidInitialization`) and would downgrade
the impl. On those chains recipient/network/min are mutable storage with owner-gated
setters, so a plain setter call is the correct, minimal mechanism — which is what this
template provides.

### Files

- **`src/template/SetFeeVaultConfig.sol`** — `L2TaskBase` template; emits one portal
  deposit per *changed* field across the configured `vaultProxies`.
- **`test/tasks/example/sep/041-set-fee-vault-config/`** — example task (OP Sepolia:
  L1FeeVault + OperatorFeeVault → shared recipient, WithdrawalNetwork.L1).
- **`test/integration/SetFeeVaultConfigIntegration.t.sol`** — end-to-end test; forks
  L1 + OP Sepolia, replays the setter deposits, asserts the vault config changed. Reuses
  `IntegrationBase`.

### Validation

- **Capability/version gate** — rejects vaults below the min version that exposes the
  setters (Sequencer/Base/L1 ≥ 1.6.0, Operator ≥ 1.1.1); old immutable vaults must use
  `FeeVaultUpgradeTemplate` first.
- **Required `l2RpcUrls` preflight** — asserts `L2 ProxyAdmin.owner() == aliased root`,
  enforces the version gate, and **dry-runs the setters** as the aliased owner so an L2
  revert surfaces at setup instead of silently on relay.
- **Per-field skip-unchanged** — only fields that differ from live state produce a deposit;
  at least one must change (else the framework reverts "No actions found").
- **`_validate`** — asserts action count + every action targets the OptimismPortal, value 0.
- Non-zero recipient, `network <= 1`, and known-vault checks.

## Test plan

- [x] `forge test --match-test test_setFeeVaultConfig_integration -vvv` — 1/1 passed (4/4 deposits succeed; recipient/network/min verified on the OP Sepolia fork)
- [x] `just simulate` on `sep/041` — `SETFEEVAULTCONFIG: VALIDATED PORTAL DEPOSIT ACTIONS`
- [x] `forge build --deny-warnings` — clean
- [x] `forge fmt --check` — clean
- [x] `./src/script/check-struct-order.sh` — clean

## Self-review (template-review checklist)

Ran the internal template-review checklist; **0 blocking findings**. Minor items resolved:
inline interfaces (`IOptimismPortal2`/`IProxyAdminView`/`IVersioned`), `vm.label`s, corrected
NatSpec (the "No actions found" behavior + skip-unchanged sign-time semantics), removed an
unused import, `Supports:` line added. `_taskStorageWrites = ["OptimismPortalProxy"]`
cross-checked against the sim state diff.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Escalation:** this is a **new template type** and performs a **cross-layer** operation
> (L1→L2 portal deposits driving L2 setter calls) — flagged for **Security-team review** per
> the template-review checklist.

## Notes

- Additive: does not modify `UpdateFeeVaultRecipient` or `FeeVaultUpgradeTemplate`.
- No `Regression.t.sol` entry: per-field skip-unchanged reads live L2 state, so a
  hardcoded-calldata regression test would be non-deterministic. The `sep/041` example is

develop's `semver-diff` check is red because #21591 landed a `semver-lock.json` entry for `OPContractsManagerStandardValidator` that was pre-computed on a branch without #21518's changes to the same contract (a semantic merge). Pre-merge CI can't catch this because the check only compares the lock against the target branch, never against the tree it's committed with.

- Bumps the validator 2.11.0 → 2.11.1 and updates the lock entry to match the merged source, unbreaking develop.
- Hardens `check-semver-diff.sh`: in CI (where the check runner regenerates the lock before this script runs) it now fails if the committed lock differs from the regenerated one, so stale-lock semantic merges are caught pre-merge and in the merge queue.

Verified locally: the hardened check passes on this branch (`✅ ... version changed from 2.11.0 to 2.11.1`) and fails with a clear diff when the stale develop lock is substituted back in.

op-node: Reject stale sequencer build starts

Fixes ethereum-optimism/optimism#21635.

When the source local-safe head advances past the follower's current unsafe head, follow-source advances both the follower's unsafe and local-safe heads to that source local-safe block. This makes the followed chain canonical in the follower's EL and can reorg out its previous unsafe tip. An already-ready sequencer timer can then run before the queued forkchoice notification, starting a payload on the removed parent. op-reth returns `missing parent header`, which op-node escalates through the deposit-only invalid-build path to a critical shutdown. CircleCI Insights reports 3 flakes with this exact ordering.

Reject non-derived build starts whose parent no longer matches the engine controller's unsafe head. The check shares the controller lock with follow-source, eliminating the stale-parent ordering before any Engine API call. A focused regression reproduces the exact downstream failure path.

op-reth: print a backtrace when an integration test dies on a signal

Stacked on #21909 — review that first; this PR's diff is the second commit only.

Makes the next recurrence of #20973 yield a faulting stack. Instrumentation only: no behavior change to any test, no effect unless a fatal signal fires.

`p2p_version::peers_negotiate_eth_69` segfaults during teardown after its body has passed. A binary killed by a signal produces no Rust backtrace — `RUST_BACKTRACE` only covers panics — so five recurrences over two months have yielded nothing beyond the signal number, and it has never reproduced locally across 570+ attempts. Investigation is stalled for want of a stack.

Core dumps can't supply one. On the CircleCI Docker executor `/proc/sys` is read-only so `core_pattern` cannot be set, and the host's pipe pattern makes the kernel write the core outside the container — verified by running an actual segfault in the base image. An in-process handler needs no privileges, no artifacts and no CI config, and works locally.

The faulting **thread name** is the payload. It discriminates directly between the candidate causes enumerated in [this analysis](https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/issues/20973#issuecomment-5023965394) — a database `atexit` destructor racing its own live threads, background threads outliving process exit, or a runtime teardown race.

Output against a simulated teardown crash:

```
=== fatal signal 11 in thread 'mdbx-rs-txn-mgr' faulting address 0x0000000000000000 ===
.../deps/flaky-58aa09ba589b158c(+0x362db) [0x560a585772db]
/usr/lib/libc.so.6(+0x3e270) [0x7f6e7d23e270]
...
```

Two details worth knowing before reviewing the handler:

**The stack is emitted in two stages, and the order is load-bearing.** `backtrace_symbols_fd` runs first: it writes straight to the fd and does not call malloc. `std::backtrace::Backtrace` runs second for names and line numbers — its symbolization allocates heavily and *faults a second time* when called from a handler, killing the process before anything is printed, since SIGSEGV is blocked inside its own handler. That was the first version of this patch, and it printed nothing at all. Attempting it only after the reliable frames are already on the wire makes that failure free. Expect the symbolized section to be empty in practice.

**It re-raises with the default disposition**, so the process still dies with the original signal and nextest still records a crash rather than a pass. That composes with #21909: nextest prints a failed attempt's stderr even when a later attempt passes, so a recurrence yields a stack while the job stays green.

Resolution is module + offset, not function names, because Rust doesn't export symbols to the dynamic table; resolve offline with `addr2line`, or add `-rdynamic` later if it proves necessary.

`libc` is already a workspace dependency; added here as a dev-dependency only.

rust: retry the eth69 teardown SIGSEGV flake

Stops `p2p_version::peers_negotiate_eth_69` from ejecting unrelated PRs from the merge queue. Mitigation only — the crash is unresolved, see #20973.

The test dies with SIGSEGV *after* its body has passed: assertions succeed, nextest prints `test result: ok`, then the binary segfaults during teardown and the run fails purely on the signal exit. Five recurrences since 2026-05.

Retrying is sound here specifically because the crash is teardown-only. Every assertion has already succeeded, and nextest reruns in a fresh process, so a pass on retry re-establishes them from scratch rather than masking a failure. The run is still reported FLAKY and the failed attempt's stderr is still printed, so recurrences stay visible.

**Why this file didn't already exist.** `rust/{op-reth,kona,op-alloy}` have no `Cargo.toml` at all and `rust/alloy-op-evm/Cargo.toml` has no `[workspace]` table — all are members of `rust/Cargo.toml`, and nextest resolves config from the workspace root. So all four of their `.config/nextest.toml` files have never been read in monorepo CI. That is why op-reth's declared `retries = 2` never applied and this flake hard-failed instead of being retried.

No `[profile.default]` base block is added, so defaults are unchanged for every other job. The filter uses `test(=...)`: bare `test(...)` is a substring match, so a later sibling such as `peers_negotiate_eth_69_disconnect` would silently inherit the retries. `binary_id(...)` would be more precise still, but nextest rejects a `binary_id` matching nothing in the current invocation as a hard config error, which would break `cargo nextest run -p <other-crate>` from `rust/`.


#21910 stacks on this and adds a crash handler, so the next recurrence yields a faulting stack.

op-deployer: build continuation deploy input from prepared state

**Description**

`op-deployer` builds continuation deployment inputs from prepared state. Permissionless chains use their committed game type, selected prestate, and complete starting-anchor proposal. Later game type or prestate changes are rejected.

`CANNON_KONA` uses the fixed permissioned fallback. `SUPER_CANNON_KONA` has no fallback prestate. Permissioned deployments keep existing behavior.

Missing or incompatible prepared values fail before execution. Re-running `prepare` clears the starting anchor for chains it predicts again. Deployed chains keep their state.

The same completed input can be used for preflight and deployment. Deployment is recorded separately, allowing `continue` to record only after broadcast succeeds.

Covers game types, prepared-state authority, fallbacks, invalid state, chain binding, anchor transport and resets, permissioned compatibility, execution and recording, and deployed configuration.
